book: 171 - House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic

chapters.relation: Argues that Marx's claim that the modern state is 'a committee for managing the common affairs of the bourgeoisie' explains House of Cards better than Frank's own power-over-money creed: Raymond Tusk and SanCorp dictate President Walker's policies and cost Frank the Secretary of State post, and even Frank's signature America Works jobs bill functions as a capitalist subsidy (government-paid wages, gutted entitlements), while the Dunbar-versus-Walmart fight over Medicaid shows the state arbitrating among capitalists. The authors conclude that even a worker victory like a Dunbar minimum-wage raise would only be a concession in an ongoing class conflict, so 'democracy is so overrated' because capital, not Frank, is really in charge of the White House.

Uses Foucault's panopticon (built on Bentham's prison design) and Bauman's 'liquid surveillance' to read Frank's Washington as a surveillance society: Zoe's archived texts, Doug's inescapable tracking of Rachel, and the bugged cell where Claire visits Michael Corrigan all show how being watched destroys privacy and paralyzes dissent. It argues that democracy needs free spaces in which citizens can question power without later punishment, so the culture of fear Frank rules through-'you are a rock, you absorb nothing, you say nothing'-turns checks and balances into instruments of control even inside an elected government.

chapters.file: ch24 - PART V INTRAPERSONAL RELATIONSHIPS, SEXUALITY, AND RACE IN HOUSE OF CARDS.md

chapters.relation: Defends the Underwoods' open marriage by applying Wasserstrom's account of adultery (wrong via promise-breaking, deception, and pain): Frank and Claire's mutually negotiated nonmonogamy-frank transparency with Claire about Zoe, Claire rushing home to Frank from Adam's-apartment avoids all three wrongs, and Punzo's dualist claim that sex merges souls is rejected as unverifiable and damaging. It reads the marriage as an egalitarian partnership whose tit-for-tat renegotiation after Claire's watershed-bill sabotage and their agreed childlessness ('I promise you freedom from that') show that nonmonogamy strengthens rather than corrodes their bond.

Argues that Freddy Hayes's storyline-Frank slumming at the BBQ joint, the franchise plan designed so white customers 'feel like they slumming', and Frank cutting Freddy loose when his son's gun photo goes viral-commodifies black male life as 'spice' for a white narrative (bell hooks) and exemplifies Nancy Leong's racial capitalism, where blackness has value only insofar as it benefits white institutions. Drawing on Tommy Curry, Michelle Alexander, and Derrick Bell's racial realism ('I live to harass white folks'), the chapter claims the show reinforces rather than interrupts the stereotype equating blackness with criminality, poverty, and death.

Reads the show through Rousseau's contrast between the general will and a pathological 'corporate will': governments and corporations are sociopathic artificial persons that depersonalize their agents, degrading natural self-love (amour de soi) into status-hungry amour-propre. On this account Frank's break with Freddy ('just a good customer'), the Tusk-Walker alliance, and Remy and Jackie's bought loyalties are Aristotelian friendships of utility or pleasure crushed under the corporate will, never true friendship, leaving Washington with 'honor without virtue' and men 'everywhere in chains'.

chapters.file: ch28 - PART VI EXISTENTIAL REALITIES SELF-LOVE AND FREEDOM.md

chapters.relation: Analyzes Frank's kneeling 'I pray to myself, for myself' as an ethics of autoeroticism built on metaphysical atheism, ruthless pragmatism, and happiness-as-power: like Glaucon's Ring of Gyges, removing God from the equation makes the murders of Zoe and Russo cost only human, never eternal, judgment. The chapter details three exercises of Machiavellian virtu-feigned piety at the Peachoid vigil, fox-like promise-breaking with Tusk, and 'cruelty well-used' toward Russo-before closing on Augustine's critique of the libido dominandi: Frank's betrayal of Freddy, met with a flash of remorse, shows the lust for domination enslaves rather than liberates, the way of the City of Man.

Contrasts Frank's ethical egoism with Beauvoir's existential ethics: Frank moves like an invisible Ring-of-Gyges wearer-murdering Zoe, reading everyone's self-interest-yet because he treats others purely as instruments his freedom is never 'prolonged through the freedom of others', and it fails in Season 3 when he miscalculates Jackie, Remy, and Claire. Claire's awakening through Michael Corrigan and her final walkout dramatize the Beauvoirian lesson that consciousness is freedom-as-nothingness whose values we remain collectively responsible for, not a license to will anything.

chapters.file: ch31 - PART VII LET ME BE FRANK WITH YOU AGENCY, AESTHETICS, AND INTENTION.md

chapters.relation: Takes up the puzzle of imaginative resistance (Gendler): while viewers would refuse to imagine that Frank's murder of Zoe was 'brave and noble', we end up rooting for his double murder and abuses of power. It explains this lack of resistance through the Greenville first-pitch confession, Frank's fourth-wall asides that grant us secret intimacy ('I despise children'), and Robinson's account of emotion-driven understanding-an engineered emotional seduction that doubles as a lesson in how politicians and artists manipulate audiences into morally deviant points of view.

Defends Bratman's planning theory of intention against Davidson's reductionism using Frank's schemes: his intention to become President is a distinct commitment-involving plan-state that imposes consistency and control-forcing him to postpone revenge on Walker, readjust when Claire derails Peter's water bill, and coordinate cross-temporally with Claire-where mere beliefs and desires cannot. Tusk's 'decisions made on emotions aren't decisions at all' and Frank's handling of the Corrigan backlash illustrate why intentions, not passions, are the inputs that keep his long-run plans on track.

Treats Frank's soliloquies-strangling the dog's 'useless pain', the Peachoid eulogy that goads a grieving congregation toward hating God, urinating on his father's grave 'to seem more human'-as a Heideggerian tour of concealment and disclosure, where truth is disclosure rather than correspondence and Frank alienates himself from responsibility and even from being human. Quoting Iris Murdoch on how fiction makes goodness seem dull and invoking Roth's 'theodicy of protest', the chapter warns that Frank's shuffling of morality into maneuver relaxes our moral guard about blame, God, and evil.

chapters.file: ch35 - PART VIII VIRTUE AND CHARACTER IN HOUSE OF CARDS.md

chapters.relation: Sorts Frank's six friendships using Aristotle's three types: Freddy and Meechum are friendships of pleasure, Doug, Durant, Tusk, and Jackie friendships of utility, while Claire-despite 'I love that woman more than sharks love blood'-cannot be a true friend of the good because true friendship requires two people of good character seeing themselves in each other. Since Aristotle ties friendship to flourishing, the chapter ends hoping that Frank, who has good fortune but neither good character nor true friends, may yet choose virtue and the good life.

Asks who is morally worse by three standards-what each has done, is doing, and would do in the future subjunctive-and answers that Frank and Claire are far worse together, read symbolically as the US Constitution itself: Frank is the mercurial House, Claire the deliberate, more ambitious Senate, and Meechum the loyal military they seduce and underestimate at the republic's peril. Working from Plato's and Aristotle's claim that democracy declines into tyranny, Niebuhr's 'moral mediocrity' of nations, and the Welch-McCarthy 'have you no decency' moment, it asks whether a system that produced them is one 'we the people' deserve.

chapters.file: ch38 - President Frank Underwood's White House Staff (Contributors).md

holes.name: Racial Capitalism
holes.what: Nancy Leong's term for deriving social and economic value from racial identity by commodifying it, so that nonwhiteness is valued only insofar as it benefits white people and institutions.
holes.why: Chapter 26's central claim is that Freddy Hayes's 'authentic' BBQ persona is exactly such a commodity, consumed by white viewers and discarded by Frank when its value drops.

holes.name: Derrick Bell
holes.what: Founder of critical race theory who defended 'racial realism', the view that racism is a permanent feature of US society, and urged defiance ('I live to harass white folks') over utopian hopes of racial equity.
holes.why: Chapter 26 closes by adopting Bell's racial realism as the stance of its own critique, refusing to hope the show's representation will ever interrupt white supremacy.

holes.name: Imaginative Resistance
holes.what: The puzzle (Tamar Szabo Gendler) of why audiences resist imagining morally deviant claims in fiction-such as a murder being 'noble'-even though they can imagine dragons and impossible worlds, explained as unwillingness rather than inability.
holes.why: Chapter 32 argues House of Cards produces a striking 'lack of imaginative resistance', seducing viewers through fourth-wall asides and emotional intimacy into rooting for Frank's murders.

holes.name: Planning Theory of Intention
holes.what: Michael Bratman's view that intentions are distinct, commitment-involving plan-states (partial, consistency-demanding, control-enabling) that organize practical reasoning over time and are irreducible to belief and desire.
holes.why: Chapter 33 is built on Bratman's antireductionism, using Frank's cross-temporal schemes and adjustable plans to show intentions doing work beliefs and desires cannot.

holes.name: Iris Murdoch
holes.what: Novelist-philosopher who argued that art fascinates by exploring the 'meaner' aspects of our being, so that sympathizing with fictional characters relaxes the moral guard and weakens our better nature.
holes.why: Chapter 34 leans on Murdoch to explain why the Peachoid eulogy and the grave-urination scene entertain rather than appall us.
